Budget 2020: Difficult decisions

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Finance minister Tito Mboweni says that tough decisions can no longer be postponed but ahead of the budget we look at how the ruling party has undermined his MTBPS as South Africa dithers ahead of a d

Unique Selling Point:
I dont know yet except to say we have some very strong opinions on how fragile our current situation is


Summary:
Summary
South Africa is on the edge of a precipice and we have run out of money. Our economic recovery has failed, the president is weak, the fightback by his enemies grows stronger by the day and all the financial wizards agree on at least one thing: Government has no choice it has to reduce expenditure. That was the message coming out of Tito’s 2019 MTBPS, but that is the message that has not been heeded by his own government.



Further information:
FURTHER INFORMATION
In Tito’s own words he tells us that SA is experiencing its lowest BUSINESS CYCLE DOWNTURN since 1945 and that there is little chance of the country’s 9.4 million unemployed adults finding a job. THE COUNTRY CANNOT WAIT ANY LONGER HE SAYS AND WARNS OF DIRE CONSEQUENCES IF THE WE DON’T MAKE DIFFICULT DECISIONS.

But the president hasn’t made those difficult decisions and Lumkile Mondi a senior economics lecturer at Wits believes we are already in serious trouble: “people don’t realise how deep in trouble we are, they think we will manage. Our probability of failure is much bigger than our probability of success. We have to realise that if we won’t take the action that is required – we have a 70% chance of failure, and that is why we have to take serious drastic structural reforms.

Many quick wins were tabled in the August treasury document and again in October. But few if any of them have materialised.

• Promote investment and job creation
• Cut the public service wage bill
• Promote tourism by reducing the cost of travelling to South Africa
• Increase tourism numbers
• Implement an electronic visa platform
• Grant licenses for small scale power generation projects
• Expand telecommunication services – open up spectrum
• Immediate reforms in transport water and telecommunications policy
• Lower the cost of business
• Promote growth in agriculture
• Strengthen road and rail
• Student housing at 3 universities - - allocated R3.4 billion
• Stabilising state- owned companies
• Fast track the renewables programme
• Reduce the claims against the state

What we see as we entered 2020 – was more retrenchments from Massmart, Arcelor Mittal, Telkom et al. The public sector wage bill has not been reduced and in fact we have just spent more money at SAA to save jobs – government is looking to the Chinese market to expand tourism. The Corona virus may have put an end to that market at least for the foreseeable future. We have increased the number of countries that are visa exempt, but not from some of our major markets – we still don’t have those licenses for small scale power generation – and the renewables round 5, 6 and 7 are held up by Minister Mantashe for approval. After a decade delay – there is now at least a plan to open spectrum but it hasn’t been implemented. -Prasa and Transnet are both in dire straights and ships avoid our ports if possible – the operations of Eskom may begin to stabilse but certainly not its finances – even as the put the entire economy at risk, and just the medical claims alone against the state are over R100 billion rand

Let’s take what happened at SAA last week when the president tried to interfere with the Business Rescue practitioner who cut routes to try and save the airline. Lumkile Mondi believes comments like those of the president and the minister of public enterprises signal a collapse of the sanctity of the treasury and gives further dire warnings:

“it means that the whole frugality and credibility of our budget system has all but collapsed. We cannot trust it, we cannot rely on it, because it’s being driven outside of processes outside of the treasury – so the treasury becomes something else then, and reminds us of our past during the apartheid regime where two sets of books were kept, and there were a lot of off balance sheet expenditures that show the apartheid regime was living beyond its means So this regime might be in the same boat that it is living beyond its means, and so therefore SA will be on the brink of collapse and running a high inflation environment because we will be funding ourselves by printing money.

Who would have thought that the mighty powerful apartheid machinery would have collapsed, at least then leadership was quick to realise that they were in deep financial trouble. We are now spending a billion rand a day servicing debt. If you are growing its fine, but where is your growth going to come from when there is no electricity? ‘

And next he warns will be prescribed assets:

“So the biggest danger is if addition to our current exposure that the state expands its ambition of not only accessing the public sector pensions but also accesses pensions of private sector we will all get poorer. There will be a huge private sector run on pension funds and it will destroy South Africans savings

Ahead of the budget we look at how government has ignored the recommendations from its own treasury.

Press Release:


Upcoming Budget: Difficult Decisions
Amid another looming downgrade, with spiralling debt, weak growth and a slow pace of reform, last year’s medium-term budget gave a clear roadmap of what the government needed to do. Finance Minister Tito Mboweni said reversing the trends required urgent action, but can he make the difficult decisions needed to save the economy?
Producer: Joy Summers | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


FINAL SCRIPT BUDGET 2020: DIFFICULT DECISIONS: TX SUNDAY 23rd Feb 2020

Commentary One
As budget day comes around again, spare a thought for finance minister Tito Mboweni, he probably has the toughest job in Cabinet

Derek Link
If you were in any doubt about just how serious South Africa’s financial position is look no further than this treasury document from October last year – it’s 86 pages of warts and all numbers that are bound to send your blood pressure rocketing

Lumkile Mondi
Time has run out. Time has run out

Commentary Two
Senior Economics lecturer at Wits, Lumkile Mondi, says we are facing a catastrophe unless the finance minister does something drastic next week

Lumkile Mondi
The president and the finance minister at the moment remain the only reformers. We need to see more coming from, for example Minister Mantashe and his colleagues to say you know what, we support the future of our children, the future of our country.

Commentary three
The country needs growth, but for the last decade growth’s gone down. Treasury revised their projection for 2019 to just 0.5%. This year is looking as bad. So, we aren’t growing, and our debt is rising. Treasury projects it to reach 71.3% of GDP by 2022/23.

Derek
Lumkile this is the SA economy MasterChef style!

Commentary Four
To keep it simple Lumkile gave me a culinary explanation

Lumkile
So in 2009 I could cut to South Africans about 70% of this cake, because only 30 % belonged to lenders, that was our debt
Derek
The rest was ours. 70% was ours?
Lumkile Mondi
Yes. Today I have only 35% left, so this portion here represents 35% of what belongs to us. What I leave on the table is what is being owed to the rest of the world.
Derek
So that 65%, that huge chunk doesn’t go to development, to infrastructure – just to servicing debt?


Lumkile
More importantly about a billion we take away from this cake to try and service this on a daily basis. So, going forward if we don’t grow, we may have very little left on that plate

Commentary Five
It’s an unnerving figure- R1 billion rand in interest alone, paid out every day to service our debt! Which is why we so desperately need growth to sweeten our numbers

Lumkile
Together with the rest of these different colours we will sweeten our GDP

LINK
Treasury says the country cannot wait any longer and they have come up with easy wins that could boost growth over the next two years which should be implemented without delay

Commentary Six
These include
PROMOTE TOURISM
REDUCE RED TAPE FOR SMALL BUSINESSES
GRANT LICENSES FOR SMALL SCALE POWER GENERATION PROJECTS
FAST TRACK THE RENEWABLES PROGRAMME
RAPIDLY EXPAND FIBRE INFRASTRUCTURE
MODERNISE PORTS AND STRENGTHEN ROAD AND RAIL
REHABILITATE MUNICIPAL INFRASTRUCTURE
PROMOTE AGRICULTURE

Lumkile Mondi
They are fantastic! but a lot of those reforms rest with the state, and we know our state is a tortoise! We need now a cheetah, we don’t need a tortoise.

Commentary Seven
9.4 million adults have little chance of finding a job says treasury. And as big companies shed thousands of jobs, emerging commercial farmer Gift Mafuleka is creating them.

Gift Mafuleka
It’s not easy to enter into mainstream commercial farming. There is a big disconnect from what government is saying to what is happening on the ground

Commentary eight
Mafuleka has a thirty- year lease from government for his 340 hectares. He began by growing grains, but soon realized the need to diversify to stay in business

Gift
What you would have seen here two years ago was long grass, weeds all over. I remember one meeting I had with then potential customer and they were very furious with me
because they said Gift you make us drive all the way from Johannesburg to just see bare land (laughs) but there was a plan!

Commentary nine
The plan was to secure a large retail contract to buy his vegetables. Then he found development funding to build this infrastructure – but what you see here came not from government funding, but from the private sector.

Gift Mafuleka
One of our new enterprises on this farm which is not more than two years old but it has created more than 15 sustainable jobs. Agriculture being a primary sector it attracts a lot of low- level jobs but those jobs keep food on the table.

Commentary ten
But all those reforms will still not be enough, says economist Dawie Roodt.

Dawie Roodt
Even if you implement all the right things, the reality is that the South African growth ceiling at the moment is less than 1 %- that is the maximum at which the South African economy can grow at the moment, and the simple reason for that is because we do not have electricity!

Commentary eleven
It’s now been four months since treasury said difficult decisions were needed to stabilize the public finances -but the two most difficult decisions are still outstanding. First, what to do with Eskom’s debt? A debt treasury describes as a massive risk to the economy.

Dawie Roodt
One big elephant in the room the president did NOT address is that- the reality is Eskom has a lot of debt -nearly R500 billion, that is roughly about 10% of the size of the SA economy.

Commentary twelve
That debt is equivalent to Gauteng’s entire budget for almost 4 years
Dawie
We are talking about a lot of money!

Commentary thirteen
The finance ministers second difficult decision: reduce the public service salary bill. That consumed 46% of our tax revenue. Recently civil servants wages grew by 10.4% while their private sector counterparts got only 2.1%

Dawie
If you really want to cut back on state spending it is inevitable that many thousands of people must lose their jobs and a lot of people will get angry. The ANC is simply not prepared to swallow that very, very bitter pill!


Commentary fourteen
Minister Mboweni announced he wanted to reduce state expenditure by R150 billion rand Four months later, he is still sucking on that bitter pill

Derek
Do you think the tough talk in this statement is already being thrown out of the window?
Lumkile Mondi
I think by some in the ANC alliance. But I am very confident that Minister Mboweni was on retirement would have gone back had he not had his way. I think in this case he has got his way; the president has announced these reforms. I think next Wednesday he is going to be the most popular man amongst those of us who want stability, but those who want to destroy, because mismanagement creates opportunities for stealing are going to be very very, unhappy.

Commentary fifteen
Our state- owned companies are also adding spending pressure says Treasury.

Plane up sound

In 2019 almost the entire contingency reserve of R10 billion for emergencies was wiped out to save SAA, SABC and Denel. And if there is a state- owned company that mirrors what’s gone wrong with our finances, its SAA.

Derek up sound greets Vuyani Jarana

In November 2017, former Vodacom executive Vuyani Jarana took a 50% pay cut to help save the airline

Derek
Did you really think you could turn SAA around?
Vuyani
To be honest with you I did and even today I still think SAA could be turned around. You need to restructure it and reconfigure it completely

Commentary seventeen
His plan was on track, but he soon found himself mired in bureaucracy and let down by government. Eighteen months later he resigned

Vuyani
The challenge is that SAA is not a government department it competes in an open market its competitors emirates, BA Comair, they make decisions in hours and days …we made decisions in months – it’s a problem, so you can’t compete in that environment

Commentary eighteen
His solution for Mboweni, is to look to small and medium enterprises to save the day.


Vuyani
The answer sits with small businesses, large businesses are not going to create jobs, technology is working against job creation at the high end

Commentary nineteen
And he is hoping for some good news to come out of the SAA business rescue.

Vuyani
I think it’s a very difficult situation they are in. The rescue process is the last card to be played, so I don’t want to pre-empt what their plan is going to be in the BRP, but I think they have a chance to emerge as a much stronger airline completely restructured, if they do the right things.

Commentary twenty
But will SAA do the right thing? Will our politicians make the difficult decisions treasury says we must? The country and the airline are on borrowed time. But can we prevail?

Vuyani
We will prevail, it needs SA to pull together. We need to spend time looking at unorthodox tactics that we can apply. I don’t think we are going to get the economy going using the same script we used during good times
Derek
Vuyani you sound optimistic, which is relatively rare
Vuyani
I am optimistic because if we pull in the right levers we can get ourselves out of the hole –
it doesn’t mean we are not in a difficult …balancing act – I wouldn’t want to be the finance minister heavy trade offs

Derek
Lumkile should we be holding onto our seats on Wednesday?
We know where you live, we know where your income is, so with no other source of revenue you are an easier target for us, so watch this space, watch Vat and other forms of taxes which will affect the middle class and upper echelons of the country

THE END. 11. 02

PROMO ONE
Its budget day on Wednesday and the finance minister has a huge hole to fill
Lumkile
Hold onto your seats on Wednesday, because you may be attacked as a taxpayer.

PROMO TWO
In October 2019 the finance minister said South Africa urgently needs to grow and we must make difficult decisions. Ahead of the budget we follow the numbers



PROMO THREE
South Africans across the board will be watching Wednesday’s budget closely. Our GDP growth has slowed and our debt is rising. Will the finance minister balance the books?

NAMES

LUMKILE MONDI
SENIOR LECTURER: WITS SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS & FINANCE

DAWIE ROODT
CHIEF ECONOMIST: EFFICIENT GROUP

GIFT MAFULEKA
DEVELOPING COMMERCIAL FARMER

VUYANI JARANA
BUSINESS TRANSFORMATION EXEC. & FORMER CEO: SAA

And if there is a state- owned company that mirrors what’s gone wrong with our finances, its SAA. Derek up sound greets Vuyani Jarana In November 2017, former Vodacom executive Vuyani Jarana took a 50% pay cut to help save the airline Derek Did you really think you could turn SAA around? Vuyani To be honest with you I did and even today I still think SAA could be turned around. You need to restructure it and reconfigure it completely Commentary seventeen His plan was on track, but he soon found himself mired in bureaucracy and let down by government. Eighteen months later he resigned Vuyani The challenge is that SAA is not a government department it competes in an open market its competitors emirates, BA Comair, they make decisions in hours and days …we made decisions in months – it’s a problem, so you can’t compete in that environment Commentary eighteen His solution for Mboweni, is to look to small and medium enterprises to save the day. Vuyani The answer sits with small businesses, large businesses are not going to create jobs, technology is working against job creation at the high end Commentary nineteen And he is hoping for some good news to come out of the SAA business rescue. Vuyani I think it’s a very difficult situation they are in. The rescue process is the last card to be played, so I don’t want to pre-empt what their plan is going to be in the BRP, but I think they have a chance to emerge as a much stronger airline completely restructured, if they do the right things. Commentary twenty But will SAA do the right thing? Will our politicians make the difficult decisions treasury says we must? The country and the airline are on borrowed time. But can we prevail? Vuyani We will prevail, it needs SA to pull together. We need to spend time looking at unorthodox tactics that we can apply. I don’t think we are going to get the economy going using the same script we used during good times Derek Vuyani you sound optimistic, which is relatively rare Vuyani I am optimistic because if we pull in the right levers we can get ourselves out of the hole – it doesn’t mean we are not in a difficult …balancing act – I wouldn’t want to be the finance minister heavy trade offs Derek Lumkile should we be holding onto our seats on Wednesday? We know where you live, we know where your income is, so with no other source of revenue you are an easier target for us, so watch this space, watch Vat and other forms of taxes which will affect the middle class and upper echelons of the country THE END. 11. 02 PROMO ONE Its budget day on Wednesday and the finance minister has a huge hole to fill Lumkile Hold onto your seats on Wednesday, because you may be attacked as a taxpayer. PROMO TWO In October 2019 the finance minister said South Africa urgently needs to grow and we must make difficult decisions. Ahead of the budget we follow the numbers PROMO THREE South Africans across the board will be watching Wednesday’s budget closely. Our GDP growth has slowed and our debt is rising. Will the finance minister balance the books? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Finance minister Tito Mboweni says that tough decisions can no longer be postponed but ahead of the budget we look at how the ruling party has undermined his MTBPS as South Africa dithers ahead of a d
metadata.Unique Selling Point: I dont know yet except to say we have some very strong opinions on how fragile our current situation is
metadata.Summary: Summary South Africa is on the edge of a precipice and we have run out of money. Our economic recovery has failed, the president is weak, the fightback by his enemies grows stronger by the day and all the financial wizards agree on at least one thing: Government has no choice it has to reduce expenditure. That was the message coming out of Tito’s 2019 MTBPS, but that is the message that has not been heeded by his own government.
metadata.Further information: FURTHER INFORMATION In Tito’s own words he tells us that SA is experiencing its lowest BUSINESS CYCLE DOWNTURN since 1945 and that there is little chance of the country’s 9.4 million unemployed adults finding a job. THE COUNTRY CANNOT WAIT ANY LONGER HE SAYS AND WARNS OF DIRE CONSEQUENCES IF THE WE DON’T MAKE DIFFICULT DECISIONS. But the president hasn’t made those difficult decisions and Lumkile Mondi a senior economics lecturer at Wits believes we are already in serious trouble: “people don’t realise how deep in trouble we are, they think we will manage. Our probability of failure is much bigger than our probability of success. We have to realise that if we won’t take the action that is required – we have a 70% chance of failure, and that is why we have to take serious drastic structural reforms. Many quick wins were tabled in the August treasury document and again in October. But few if any of them have materialised. • Promote investment and job creation • Cut the public service wage bill • Promote tourism by reducing the cost of travelling to South Africa • Increase tourism numbers • Implement an electronic visa platform • Grant licenses for small scale power generation projects • Expand telecommunication services – open up spectrum • Immediate reforms in transport water and telecommunications policy • Lower the cost of business • Promote growth in agriculture • Strengthen road and rail • Student housing at 3 universities - - allocated R3.4 billion • Stabilising state- owned companies • Fast track the renewables programme • Reduce the claims against the state What we see as we entered 2020 – was more retrenchments from Massmart, Arcelor Mittal, Telkom et al. The public sector wage bill has not been reduced and in fact we have just spent more money at SAA to save jobs – government is looking to the Chinese market to expand tourism. The Corona virus may have put an end to that market at least for the foreseeable future. We have increased the number of countries that are visa exempt, but not from some of our major markets – we still don’t have those licenses for small scale power generation – and the renewables round 5, 6 and 7 are held up by Minister Mantashe for approval. After a decade delay – there is now at least a plan to open spectrum but it hasn’t been implemented. -Prasa and Transnet are both in dire straights and ships avoid our ports if possible – the operations of Eskom may begin to stabilse but certainly not its finances – even as the put the entire economy at risk, and just the medical claims alone against the state are over R100 billion rand Let’s take what happened at SAA last week when the president tried to interfere with the Business Rescue practitioner who cut routes to try and save the airline. Lumkile Mondi believes comments like those of the president and the minister of public enterprises signal a collapse of the sanctity of the treasury and gives further dire warnings: “it means that the whole frugality and credibility of our budget system has all but collapsed. We cannot trust it, we cannot rely on it, because it’s being driven outside of processes outside of the treasury – so the treasury becomes something else then, and reminds us of our past during the apartheid regime where two sets of books were kept, and there were a lot of off balance sheet expenditures that show the apartheid regime was living beyond its means So this regime might be in the same boat that it is living beyond its means, and so therefore SA will be on the brink of collapse and running a high inflation environment because we will be funding ourselves by printing money. Who would have thought that the mighty powerful apartheid machinery would have collapsed, at least then leadership was quick to realise that they were in deep financial trouble. We are now spending a billion rand a day servicing debt. If you are growing its fine, but where is your growth going to come from when there is no electricity? ‘ And next he warns will be prescribed assets: “So the biggest danger is if addition to our current exposure that the state expands its ambition of not only accessing the public sector pensions but also accesses pensions of private sector we will all get poorer. There will be a huge private sector run on pension funds and it will destroy South Africans savings Ahead of the budget we look at how government has ignored the recommendations from its own treasury.
